prompt: Which part of a Bigtable table has to exist before a row can write to it?
hint: Look at what `cbt set` refused.

choices.text: Every column qualifier the rows will carry
choices.why: Qualifiers are written with the data; c-18's `o-10004` was never declared.

choices.text: The column family
choices.why: Right. A family is declared on the table, and a write to `x:note` was refused because `x` did not exist.

choices.text: The type of each value, string or integer
choices.why: There are no types: every value is bytes.

choices.text: The range of row keys the table will hold
choices.why: Row keys are never declared; any string of bytes is a valid key.

prompt: c-18 has the columns `o:o-10004` and `o:o-10005` and c-17 has neither. What does the table store for c-17's missing order columns?
hint: Bigtable is called sparse for a reason.

choices.text: An empty cell for each, so that the rows line up
choices.why: Rows do not line up; each one is its own map, and nothing is stored to make them match.

choices.text: A null marker in the family `o`
choices.why: There is no null in Bigtable. An absent column is simply absent.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right. A column a row does not have costs nothing, which is what lets a qualifier be named after an order id.

choices.text: One empty version per column, until the policy collects it
choices.why: No version is written for a column nobody wrote, so there is nothing for a policy to collect.

prompt: After `cbt set customers c-18 o:o-10004=4290`, what is in the cell?
hint: Every value in Bigtable is the same kind of thing.

choices.text: A 64-bit integer, because the value is all digits
choices.why: `cbt` does not guess types. A program that wants an integer writes a fixed-width one itself.

choices.text: The characters 4, 2, 9 and 0, as bytes
choices.why: Right. Values, row keys and qualifiers are all bytes, and `cbt set` writes what it was given as a string.

choices.text: A number the server will add to on the next write
choices.why: That is an aggregate family, a different kind of family; `o` is a plain one.

choices.text: A string, with its type recorded beside it in the family
choices.why: A family records a garbage collection policy, not a type for its values.

prompt: Which of these does one write to Bigtable guarantee? Choose every one that it does.
hint: Atomicity in Bigtable stops at the edge of a row.

choices.text: Every cell it sets in that one row is applied together, or none is
choices.why: Yes. A write to one row is atomic however many cells it touches.

choices.text: A row key nobody wrote before is created by the write
choices.why: Yes. A row exists as soon as it has a cell; there is no insert step.

choices.text: Two rows sent in one `bulk_mutate_rows` succeed or fail together
choices.why: Each row in a batch is applied on its own, and failures are reported per row.

choices.text: An index on a new column is updated in the same step
choices.why: There are no secondary indexes; the row key is the only one.

choices.text: The write is refused if its qualifier is new to the table
choices.why: New qualifiers are the normal case; only an unknown family is refused.

prompt: A family has no garbage collection policy. What happens to the older versions of a column?
hint: The policy is what removes them.

choices.text: Only the newest is kept, and each write replaces it
choices.why: That is a relational `UPDATE`. In Bigtable a write adds a cell above the old ones.

choices.text: They are kept until something deletes them
choices.why: Right. Without a policy nothing is collected, and the family grows with every write.

choices.text: They expire after thirty days, the default
choices.why: There is no default age; `ls` showed an empty policy for `p` and `o`.

choices.text: They are merged into one cell at the next compaction
choices.why: Compaction is when collection happens, and with no policy there is nothing to collect.

prompt: The policy is `maxage=30d or maxversions=2` and today is 30 October. A column has one cell, written on 29 August. What does garbage collection do with it?
hint: An age rule does not ask how many versions there are.

choices.text: Keeps it, because it is the only version
choices.why: That is what took Ana's name: the age rule is applied to every cell, the only one included.

choices.text: Deletes it, because it is older than thirty days
choices.why: Right. With `or`, either rule condemns a cell, and 62 days is past 30.

choices.text: Keeps it until a third version is written
choices.why: The version rule would keep it, but with `or` the age rule alone is enough to delete it.

choices.text: Deletes it only if the rules had been joined with `and`
choices.why: With `and`, a cell must be condemned by both; this one is the newest version, so `and` would keep it.

prompt: A family has the policy `maxage=30d and maxversions=2`, an intersection. On 30 October one column holds cells dated 15 October, 14 October, 12 October and 21 September. How many cells survive garbage collection?
hint: With `and`, a cell goes only when it is beyond the second version AND older than thirty days.

prompt: A program that writes a cell's timestamp in milliseconds, where Bigtable expects ___, stores the cell in January 1970.
hint: Count the digits in `1788000000000000`.

prompt: A family keeps `maxversions=1`, yet the program that shows a customer's current district still reads with `cells-per-column=1`. Why?
hint: When does collection happen?

choices.text: Without the filter the read is refused
choices.why: Reads without a filter are accepted; the first `lookup` of the section returned every version.

choices.text: Collection is late, and condemned cells still come back
choices.why: Right. A read can return cells the policy has already condemned, and the filter is what guarantees one version.

choices.text: The filter is what makes the read cheaper on the bill
choices.why: Bigtable bills nodes by the hour, not reads; the filter changes what comes back.

choices.text: It tells Bigtable to collect the garbage before it reads
choices.why: No read triggers collection; it happens in the background on its own schedule.

prompt: Why does the click key put a `#` between the customer and the time?
hint: Think about two thousand customers and a prefix.

choices.text: Because Bigtable splits a key into fields at `#`
choices.why: Bigtable knows nothing about `#`; the key is one string of bytes and the separator is a convention.

choices.text: So that `prefix=c-17` no longer matches c-170 too
choices.why: Right. `prefix=c-17` returned 497 rows from 111 customers, and `prefix=c-17#` the six that were c-17's.

choices.text: So that each customer's rows sort after the customer table
choices.why: The clicks table has no other kind of row; the separator is about prefixes.

choices.text: Because a row key may not hold two numbers side by side
choices.why: A row key may hold any bytes at all.

prompt: With the fifteen rows of "Loading it", how many rows does `cbt read clicks start=c-17#8207812900000 end=c-18#` return?
hint: List the keys in order, start where the start would sort, and stop before `c-18#`.

prompt: Support wants c-17's checkout events, newest first, and nothing else, as one contiguous read. Which key does it, and what does it cost?
hint: A field moved into the key decides which rows sit together.

choices.text: `c-17#checkout#<reversed time>`, and C1 then needs one read per screen
choices.why: Right. Promoting the screen groups a customer's checkouts, and the latest events of all screens are no longer one run.

choices.text: A family per screen, and every other read stays the same
choices.why: Families divide the columns inside a row; they do not choose which rows are adjacent.

choices.text: The same key with a `regex` on the screen, at no cost
choices.why: A filter reads the whole range it is given; it decides what comes back, not what is read.

choices.text: The customer id reversed, so that checkouts sort first
choices.why: Reversing the id changes where a customer's rows sit, not which of them are checkouts.

prompt: `prefix=c-17#` saw 6 rows and `regex='c-17#.*'` saw 8,999, and both returned the same 6. What explains the difference?
hint: Which of the two told the server where to start?

choices.text: The regex also matched c-170 to c-179, and dropped them
choices.why: `c-17#` cannot match `c-170#…`; the regex matched the same six rows.

choices.text: The emulator keeps a cache for prefix reads
choices.why: Both reads went to the same in-memory table; the difference is in what was read.

choices.text: A regex is a filter over the range read, and no range was given
choices.why: Right. With no start, end or prefix the range is the whole table, and the filter ran over every row.

choices.text: The regex read every version of every cell as well
choices.why: The cell counts are twice the row counts in both reads, one version of two columns each.

prompt: Why does reversing the timestamp of a time-first key not remove the hot spot?
hint: Where does the newest key sort when the time is reversed?

choices.text: Reversed keys are hashed, and so they collide
choices.why: Nothing is hashed; the key is compared byte by byte, reversed or not.

choices.text: Bigtable cannot split a tablet that holds reversed keys
choices.why: Bigtable splits any tablet; the problem is that the hot point keeps moving with the clock.

choices.text: Every new key is the smallest, so all writes go to the first tablet
choices.why: Right. The model sent all 1,000 to tablet 0; the hot spot moved from the end to the start.

choices.text: Reversed keys are longer and fill each tablet faster
choices.why: They are the same 13 digits.

prompt: A table's key is time first. The cluster sits at its autoscaling maximum of 6 nodes and the write rate will not rise. What will raising the maximum to 12 do?
hint: How many tablets are receiving the writes?

choices.text: Double the write rate, since writes spread over the nodes
choices.why: Writes spread by key range, and every new key is in one range.

choices.text: Little: every new write still goes to the one last tablet
choices.why: Right. A tablet is served by one node at a time, so more nodes add capacity nothing uses.

choices.text: Spread the hot tablet's rows over the six new nodes
choices.why: A split leaves the newest key in one tablet; the old rows spread and the writes do not.

choices.text: Make Bigtable add a salt to the keys on its own
choices.why: Bigtable never changes a key; the key is the program's.

prompt: Match each key design to where the model put one minute of new clicks.
hint: Ask where the newest key sorts in each design.

pairs.right: at the newest end of each bucket

prompt: Why does the lesson's salt come from a hash of the customer id rather than from a random digit?
hint: Think about the reader, not the writer.

choices.text: So the reader knows which bucket holds each customer
choices.why: Right. c-17 is always in bucket 8, so C1 stays one prefix read; a random salt would mean reading all ten.

choices.text: Because a random digit would send every write to one bucket
choices.why: A random digit spreads writes at least as well; the cost of it falls on the reads.

choices.text: Because Bigtable refuses keys that start with a random number
choices.why: Bigtable accepts any bytes as a key.

choices.text: So that every bucket comes out with exactly the same load
choices.why: The model's buckets were uneven, 0 to 200 a tablet; a hash spreads, it does not equalise.

prompt: Three Enterprise nodes in São Paulo at $0.98 per node-hour for 730 hours, plus a second cluster of three nodes in another zone of the same region. What is the month's node bill, in dollars?
hint: Replication between clusters in one region is not charged; the nodes are.

prompt: A Bigtable cluster serves no request all weekend. What do its nodes cost for those hours?
hint: Read the pricing page's sentence about usage.

choices.text: Nothing, since no request was made
choices.why: That is a per-request service like Firestore; Bigtable bills nodes that exist.

choices.text: The same as any other hour
choices.why: Right. Nodes are billed each hour they exist, in the page's words regardless of node usage.

choices.text: Half, at a reduced rate for an idle node
choices.why: There is no idle rate on the page.

choices.text: Only the storage, because idle nodes are paused
choices.why: Bigtable never pauses a node on its own; a node removed is a node changed by you or by autoscaling.

prompt: Why does autoscaling arrive late for a promotion that starts at 18:00 sharp?
hint: What has to happen before a new node helps?

choices.text: It runs only once an hour, on the billing boundary
choices.why: It reacts to the CPU target continuously; the hour is how nodes are billed, not when they are added.

choices.text: It waits for the storage target before adding nodes
choices.why: The CPU target alone is enough to add nodes.

choices.text: New nodes help only once tablets move onto them
choices.why: Right. The documentation warns of up to about twenty minutes under load, so the minimum is raised before the event.

choices.text: It cannot add a node while the cluster is busy
choices.why: Busy is exactly when it adds them; the delay is in the node becoming useful.

prompt: Put the steps of designing the click table in the order this lesson takes them.
hint: The table is not the first step, and neither is the key.
items: Write the questions with their inputs and sizes
Choose which field goes first in the row key
Fix the separator and the width of each part
Create the table, with its families and their policies
Load rows and read each question as a prefix or a range

prompt: A monitoring table holds one row per sensor per minute, and its main read is every sensor in the last ten minutes. Which key fits?
hint: The main read starts from a time, not from a sensor, and writes must not pile up at one end.

choices.text: The sensor, then the reversed time, read with one prefix
choices.why: That serves one sensor's history; every sensor at once would be a read of the whole table.

choices.text: The time, then the sensor, with more nodes added
choices.why: Every write lands at the end of the table, and more nodes serve tablets nobody writes to.

choices.text: A salt from the sensor, then the time, read as one range per bucket
choices.why: Right. The reads stay ranges of time, and the writes go to as many places as there are buckets.

choices.text: A hash of the whole key, read with a regex filter
choices.why: Hashing the whole key loses the order, so the read becomes a scan with a filter.

prompt: One table must keep each click for ninety days and each customer's name for as long as the account exists. How are its families arranged?
hint: A policy belongs to a family, and it is applied to every cell in it.

choices.text: One family with `maxage=90d or maxversions=1`
choices.why: The age rule would delete every name ninety days after it was written, as it took Ana's.

choices.text: Two: clicks under `maxage=90d`, names under `maxversions=1`
choices.why: Right. The name's family has no age rule, so its one version stays; the clicks expire on their own.

choices.text: One family with no policy, and a job that deletes old clicks
choices.why: That works and turns retention into a program somebody has to keep running; a policy does it on its own.

choices.text: Two families, both under `maxage=90d`
choices.why: Then the names expire too; the family that holds them must carry no age rule.
